JOURNAL

Writing Sadness Without Drowning in It

2026.09.16

Most of Yu Stellar's songs carry a little sadness, but writing sadness actually requires a certain distance — get too close and you drown in it, and whatever gets written loses its shape; stay too far away and it starts to feel fake, like borrowing someone else's grief for effect.

A more accurate way to put it might be: let yourself really feel sad first, all the way through, and only then sit down to write. Once the tears have dried and the feeling has settled a little, there's finally a way to turn that messy emotion into a lyric someone else can actually understand.

That difference decides whether a song ends up as venting or as company. Venting only really helps the person who wrote it, but company can be left behind for anyone else who happens to be sad at the same time. What Yu Stellar wants to write is the second kind.

So even when a lyric sounds painful, the moment it was written down is often already the moment the feeling started being put somewhere safe — not the moment still stuck inside it. Once sadness has been turned into a song, in a way, it's already been taken care of.
